## VNQ standalone — a high-yield but high-risk equity proxy

| Metric | VNQ | SPY |
|---|--:|--:|
| CAGR (2004–2026) | **+7.3%** | **+10.9%** |
| Annualised vol | 28.5% | 18.9% |
| Sharpe (excess-of-SHY) | **0.32** | **0.53** |
| Max drawdown | **−73.1%** | −55.2% |

VNQ delivered **lower returns, much higher volatility, and a deeper drawdown** than plain SPY
over the full joint window. The GFC peak-to-trough loss of −73.1% for VNQ vs −55.2% for SPY
already signals the direction of the crisis-diversification finding.

## Does a REIT sleeve improve the 60/40? (primary test)

Three annually-rebalanced portfolios, 1 bp one-way cost at each rebalance:

| Portfolio | CAGR | Ann. vol | Sharpe (ex-SHY) | Max DD | Worst year |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **60/20/20 SPY/VNQ/TLT (REIT sleeve)** | +9.3% | 14.8% | **0.534** | −45.7% | −22.7% |
| **60/40 SPY/TLT (baseline)** | +8.6% | 10.5% | **0.651** | −27.6% | −23.4% |
| **100% SPY** | +10.9% | 18.9% | 0.527 | −55.2% | −36.8% |

**The REIT sleeve hurt the 60/40 on every risk-adjusted metric that matters:**

- The Sharpe ratio fell from **0.651 to 0.534** (−0.117 points).
- Max drawdown worsened from **−27.6% to −45.7%** — the REIT sleeve took on 18 extra
  percentage points of downside.
- CAGR was only marginally higher (+0.7 pp) but on much more volatile returns.

### Inference

| Comparison | HAC *t* (annual diff) | Notes |
|---|--:|---|
| REIT sleeve vs 60/40 | **+1.40** | CAGR higher but not stat. significant |
| REIT sleeve vs SPY | **−1.83** | Sleeve underperforms SPY on Sharpe |

- **Bootstrap 95% CI on Sharpe difference (sleeve − 60/40):** [−0.254, +0.033], with the sleeve
  winning in only **6.1%** of resamples. The raw CAGR gain is more than offset by the extra vol
  and drawdown — the sleeve is dominated by the 60/40 on risk-adjusted terms.
- At HAC *t* = +1.40, the marginal CAGR improvement (driven by VNQ's higher loading to equity
  beta) does not reach the inference bar — and it collapses entirely on Sharpe.

## VNQ's equity correlation — the diversification claim's Achilles heel

| Window | VNQ–SPY correlation |
|---|--:|
| Full-sample (2004–2026) | **0.745** |
| Rolling 63-day (min / mean / max) | 0.042 / 0.647 / 0.945 |
| Rolling 252-day (min / mean / max) | 0.285 / 0.685 / 0.903 |
| VNQ–TLT | −0.149 |
| VNQ–GLD | +0.059 |

At **0.75 full-sample correlation with SPY**, VNQ is far more like a levered, income-paying
equity than a diversifying asset class. The rolling correlation rarely dips below 0.3 except in
brief idiosyncratic episodes. A true diversifier should sit below ~0.5 and ideally go negative
in crises — VNQ does the opposite.

## Crisis episode breakdown — VNQ piles on when it hurts most

SPY drawdown episodes deeper than −15%, with contemporaneous VNQ, TLT, and GLD returns:

| Peak | Trough | SPY | VNQ | TLT | GLD | VNQ vs SPY |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|---|
| 2007-10-09 | 2009-03-09 (GFC) | −55.2% | **−69.3%** | +25.1% | +23.9% | worse |
| 2018-09-20 | 2018-12-24 | −19.3% | −11.1% | +4.5% | +5.0% | *better* |
| 2020-02-19 | 2020-03-23 (COVID) | −33.7% | **−41.5%** | +14.2% | −3.6% | worse |
| 2022-01-03 | 2022-10-12 (rate shock) | −24.5% | **−31.9%** | −29.3% | −7.3% | worse |
| 2025-02-19 | 2025-04-08 | −18.8% | −12.5% | +0.8% | +1.6% | *better* |

**VNQ cushioned (outperformed SPY by >5pp) in 2 of 5 episodes.** In the three largest crises —
the GFC, COVID crash, and 2022 rate shock — VNQ **amplified** the equity drawdown. TLT and GLD
were the genuine diversifiers (TLT positive in 4 of 5, GLD positive in 4 of 5). VNQ behaved
more like a leveraged equity vehicle than a real-asset hedge. The 2022 episode is particularly
telling: rising interest rates simultaneously hurt equity valuations AND REIT cap rates, making
VNQ worse than SPY in a regime where the "inflation hedge" narrative suggests it should shine.

## Inflation-hedge claim — CPI regime analysis

Annual mean returns by CPI tercile (years 2004–2026):

| CPI regime | VNQ mean ann. return | SPY mean ann. return | n years |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Low inflation (< 1.7%) | +9.3% | +15.3% | 3 |
| Medium inflation | +12.4% | +12.9% | 13 |
| High inflation (> 5.5%) | **−2.7%** | −0.0% | 4 |

VNQ **underperformed** in every CPI regime relative to the "real-asset" story it sells. In high
inflation years (the inflation-hedge use case) it averaged **−2.7%** vs SPY's −0.0%. The
mechanism is clear: rising inflation forces up interest rates, which lift the discount rate on
REIT cash flows — a double negative (equity-like sensitivity to rate rises *plus* cap-rate
expansion). The CPI sample is thin (n=4 high-inflation years), so this finding is directional
rather than definitive — but it unambiguously fails to support the inflation-hedge claim.

## Verdict

- **Signal — MIXED.** VNQ is a real-assets vehicle with genuine income (CAGR +7.3% over 20
  years) and its addition to a 60/40 raises CAGR marginally — but the *risk-adjusted* effect
  is **negative** (Sharpe falls −0.117, drawdown worsens by 18 pp), and the HAC *t* on the
  CAGR difference is only +1.40, not clearing the inference bar. The signal is real (VNQ does
  earn income) but the diversification and inflation-hedge *claims* are not.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** The nominal CAGR edge is too thin, too volatile, and too drawdown-
  prone to be of practical use. The Sharpe improvement over 60/40 is negative; the bootstrap
  CI overwhelmingly favours the 60/40 (93.9% of resamples). A REIT sleeve is tradable as an
  income vehicle but not as a diversifier or hedge.
- **Inflation hedge? — BUSTED.** In the four high-CPI years in the joint window, VNQ averaged
  −2.7% while SPY averaged +0.0%. Interest-rate sensitivity dominates the real-asset story.
